messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,\qquad M=k!,\qquad N=n!.
\]

We need

\[
n \mid M^N+450.
\]

### 1. Prime factors \(p\le k\)

Suppose \(p^a\mid n\) with \(p\le k\). Then \(p\mid k!\), so

\[
v_p(M^N)=N v_p(M)\ge N.
\]

Since \(p^a\mid n\), we have \(a\le N\), so \(p^a\mid M^N\). Therefore

\[
M^N+450\equiv 450 \pmod{p^a}.
\]

Thus for divisibility by \(n\), we must have

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

Since

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2,
\]

any prime factor of \(n\) that is at most \(k\) must be \(2,3,\) or \(5\), with exponents bounded by those in \(450\).

### 2. Prime factors \(p>k\)

Now suppose \(p\mid n\) is prime and \(p>k\). Then \(p\nmid k!\). Also \(p-1\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). Hence by Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
(k!)^{n!}+450\equiv 451 \pmod p,
\]

so \(p\mid 451\). Since

\[
451=11\cdot 41,
\]

any prime factor of \(n\) exceeding \(k\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

Also, \(n\) can have at most one prime factor greater than \(k\), because two such prime factors would make \(n\ge (k+1)^2\), contradicting \(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor=k\).

So every solution has the form

\[
n=sq,
\]

where \(q\in\{1,11,41\}\), and if \(q>1\), then \(q>k\). All prime factors of \(s\) are at most \(k\), so by the first part,

\[
s\mid 450.
\]

Also, since \(q>k\), we have \(n<q^2\), so \(s<q\).

Now check cases:

- If \(q=1\), then \(n=s\le 450\).
- If \(q=11\), then \(s<11\), and the largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(11\) is \(10\), giving \(n\le 110\).
- If \(q=41\), then \(s<41\), and the largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\), giving

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

Thus any solution satisfies \(n\le 1230\).

### 3. Verification for \(n=1230\)

We have

\[
\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

and

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

For \(p=2,3,5\), since \(p\mid 35!\),

\[
35!^{1230!}\equiv 0 \pmod p,
\]

and \(450\equiv 0\pmod p\).

For \(p=41\), since \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\),

\[
35!^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]

Also

\[
450\equiv -1 \pmod{41},
\]

so

\[
35!^{1230!}+450\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]

Therefore \(1230\) divides the expression.

Hence the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
